summary.text: 门 is the simplified form of 門, meaning “gate” or “door.” The traditional graph depicts a gate; its paired-leaf appearance is clear, but whether it began as a whole gate picture or as two 戶 remains disputed.

formation.text: 門 is pictographic: its graph represents a gate with opposing leaves, sometimes shown with a lintel. A competing analysis parses it as two 戶, or door leaves; the original graphic construction remains disputed.

components.text: 門 is read as a gate with opposing leaves, sometimes including a lintel. The historical parsing into two 戶 is one analysis; another treats it as a whole gate picture, so this component records the graph as a whole.

history.text: 門 is indexed in oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and Small Seal forms. The curated oracle-bone-style image is a modern redraw whose paired uprights and crossbars suggest opposing leaves; it does not establish a sequence of graphic changes.
门 is identified as the simplified counterpart of 門; the graphic changes involved are not detailed here.

uncertainties.text: The traditional graph is analyzed either as a whole gate picture or as two 戶; another modern analysis classifies it as a semantic compound. These accounts do not resolve the original design.
Reported early gate examples and later uses do not establish an exact first attestation or a dated sequence of meanings.

senses.period: oracle-bone corpus examples; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone corpus examples are reported using 門 for gates, including a temple gate and a hall gate. They attest the gate meaning but do not establish the graph’s first occurrence.
A verbal use meaning “to attack a city gate” is reported. Its relation to the gate noun and its chronology are unresolved.
Uses meaning “path” or “key point” are reported, but their chronology and connection to the gate sense are unresolved.
Uses meaning “lineage” or “category” are reported, but their chronology and semantic path from the gate sense are unresolved.
Current glosses include “gate,” “door,” “entrance,” and “opening”; they do not establish a chronology among these meanings.

developments.text: A verbal use is reported alongside the gate noun, but no historical transition is established.
A connection to the gate sense is plausible, but no semantic development is established.
The reported uses are not linked to the gate sense by an established historical transition.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish an exact earliest attestation or a dated chronology for later senses.
